findings.where: 02-architecture.md:63,65; docs/contracts/epic-planning-ref.md:183,601; resources/planning-publication/ref-custody-helper-intents.schema.json:13,44; resources/planning-publication/ref-custody-helper-wire.schema.json:138,1017 vs 02-architecture.md:87,429; docs/contracts/epic-staging.md:15,34; 01-core-flows.md:302; 04-decisions.md:1015 (ADR-088); src/host/staging-driver.mjs:104,183,206
findings.what: The staging ref's writer contradicts the custody boundary. 02 §2 makes the separate-account ref-custody helper the sole writer of refs/autosk/** and their reflogs, and says project and model accounts cannot invoke Git mutations. epic-planning-ref.md obligation 39 requires proof that direct writes to refs/autosk/** fail from extension, model and project accounts. ADR-087/088 put the staging ref at refs/autosk/epics/<epic_ref_key>/staging, and epic-staging §1 and 01 §7 call that prefix helper-owned. Yet the helper's closed protocol has no staging action: its actions are init, create_keepalive, advance_planning, ensure_audit_ref, delete_live_ref and delete_expired_audit, and its ref pattern admits only planning, candidates/<id> and audit/candidates/<id>. Meanwhile ADR-088, 02 §2/§7 and epic-staging §1 normatively give the host's applyDelta/swapTarget, createStaging and cleanupStaging the write, as a direct `git update-ref` create, CAS and delete. Either the host's staging writes must fail (apply_staging and every re-stage after target_moved, foreign_target_movement or completion_predicate_unmet cannot run), or the 'sole writer' guarantee is false. Round 6 did not raise this, and neither ADR-087/088 nor the package's not-claimed list names it.

findings.where: docs/contracts/integration-authorization.md:9,11,43; 01-core-flows.md:298,380; docs/contracts/epic-staging.md:24,52; src/host/staging-acceptance.mjs:199 vs :239; resources/epic-staging/epic-staging.schema.json acceptance (no record reference); graph cond_441/cond_444
findings.what: On the default (human) path, the IntegrationAuthorizationRecord has no producer, no link and no defined signature. IA §1 and 01 §7 say the human's acceptance 'produces the record', and that the authority is a signed UserDecisionRecord without which a record 'authorizes nothing'. cond_441/cond_444 require integrate_staging to check the acceptance's authorization. But acceptanceFromDecision writes only {kind:'human', decision_id}. The acceptance schema has no field naming a record. No document says who mints the record on this path. And the human UDR's payload_hash signs the answer payload, whereas the auto-policy path requires record.payload_hash == authorizationPayloadHash(authorization). So on the human path the record's fields — expires_at, run_id, integration_plan_hash, the heads, ordered_ticket_commit_oids, previous_authorization_head_hash — are never under the user's signature. An integrateApproved that applies one rule would either refuse every human-path record or accept unsigned authorization fields on the one irreversible step.

findings.where: docs/contracts/epic-staging.md:32; 03-technical-plan.md:1391; 04-decisions.md:1139 (risk 11), 1034 (ADR-089); src/host/staging-lineage.mjs:61-105
findings.what: Serializing Epics per target is asserted with no state-machine mechanism. The docs say the second of two unintegrated Epics on one target 'waits until the first lands'. No step, blocker or park reason represents that wait. crossEpicErrors, the only detector, has no caller outside tests. It emits foreign_target_movement, which parks only at integrate_staging and resumes only by a human re-stage decision onto a moved target. And because a first stage must have recorded_target_base = planning.base_oid, two Epics planned from the same target head necessarily share a base, so crossEpicErrors flags them, although its own doc comment says they 'may run at once'. This is a liveness gap on the integration path with a local fix: a wait step or blocker plus a caller.

findings.where: 02-architecture.md:65 vs 02-architecture.md:87 and :429; docs/contracts/epic-staging.md §1 (line 15 'helper-owned prefix' vs 'applyDelta, which moves only the private staging ref'); 04-decisions.md ADR-088; src/host/staging-driver.mjs:104 (createStaging), :183 (swapTarget via applyDelta), :206 (cleanupStaging); src/host/planning-driver.mjs:131 (advanceRef); resources/planning-publication/ref-custody-helper-wire.schema.json (closed actions: init, create_keepalive, advance_planning, ensure_audit_ref, delete_live_ref, delete_expired_audit)
findings.what: Debt 10b fixed who moves the target ref but made the host a second writer of the helper-owned prefix. 02 §2 says project and model accounts cannot invoke Git mutations and that the separate-account ref-custody helper is the sole writer of refs/autosk/** and their reflogs. It also says bootstrap proves that direct ref probes are denied. The staging ref refs/autosk/epics/<epic_ref_key>/staging is under that prefix, and epic-staging §1 itself calls the prefix helper-owned. Yet ADR-088, 02 §7 (lines 87 and 429) and epic-staging §1 have the host's applyDelta move the staging ref. The host drivers create, CAS and delete it with direct `git update-ref`, and planning-driver.advanceRef writes the planning ref the same way. The helper's closed six-action protocol has no staging action, so no permitted writer exists for create, apply, re-stage or cleanup of staging. Under the supported layout apply_staging → integrate_staging cannot run as specified, and if the host writes anyway, the 'sole writer' guarantee is false. The package §5 discloses that the helper is absent but not that the host drivers write refs/autosk/** directly. An implementer following ADR-088 builds exactly the direct writer 02 §2 forbids.

findings.where: 02-architecture.md:63-67 (§2 Git), 03-technical-plan.md:1837-1838 (§9 Slice 1), 04-decisions.md:213 (ADR-023 rationale) vs docs/contracts/platform-support.md:51-57 (§5) and resources/platform-support/platform-support.v1.json:154-164 (install); README.md (goals, §Граница текущей работы)
findings.what: The design's enforceable boundaries rest on an install topology that the v1 packaging contract rules out. 02 §2 and 03 §9 require three things: a separate-account `autosk-flow-ref-custody` service as the sole writer of refs/autosk/**; a 'privileged install' that turns each project's common Git directory into a service-owned object database with root/helper-owned ancestors, where 'project/model accounts cannot ... invoke Git mutations'; and, per ADR-023, a signer in a separate OS account or boundary. The #13 platform contract, which is required_for_v1, says the helper ships as exactly three binaries (autosk, autoskd, autosk-store-lock) 'owned by the installing user', and its closed install record lists no helper for another account, no service account and no privileged step. An implementer who follows the packaging contract would run the ref helper and the signer as the same user as the model processes, so the boundary 02 relies on never exists. On the intent side, taking away the user's own write access to their repository's .git is a major user-visible scope decision. Neither README's goals nor any matrix obligation (#5's is 'implement crash-safe publication', #13's names no service account) states it.

findings.what: Debt 10g gave carrier keys a lifecycle, and mappingFor refuses non-v1 keys. The artifact registry got no equivalent. The five post-v1 capabilities (#28, #29, #30, #31, #33) and the out-of-matrix #47 own eight classes, and all eight are registered as ordinary active classes. The registry schema has no lifecycle field. classify() will return 'classified' for a file at, say, docs/autosk/epics/*/autobuild/*/run.json and route it to planning_ref publication with human approval, for a capability whose workflow v1 does not register. findings.where: 01-core-flows.md §7 (preamble and step 5); docs/contracts/integration-authorization.md §1, §3, §5; docs/contracts/epic-staging.md:91; src/host/staging-acceptance.mjs:181-200 vs 225-264; src/host/epic-staging.mjs:123-124; resources/program-capabilities/matrix.v1.json:240 (#9)
findings.what: On the default path, where a person accepts the staging identity, the design says the acceptance 'produces' the signed IntegrationAuthorizationRecord (IA), and that the Epic's target CAS never runs without one (ADR-088). No mechanism for this exists. The person's UserDecisionRecord signs decisionPayloadHash({option_id, identities}), with subject_hash equal to the staging identity. It does not sign the IA fields that IA §3 calls load-bearing: expires_at, integration_plan_hash, controlling_anchor_digest, the authority, dependency and intent head hashes, and previous_authorization_head_hash. The repository's only rule for 'the UserDecisionRecord behind an IA' (assertAuthorized: payload_hash === authorizationPayloadHash(authorization)) would refuse every IA made on this path. The alternative leaves those fields asserted by the daemon and not signed by the user. The host's casAdmission admits a 'human' acceptance whose decision_id is any non-empty string. epic-staging.md §5 says the person's path has no host-side check. The daemon check that is left (integrateApproved against integration_authorization_head) appears in no matrix owner's obligation: #9 names only the authority projection and the dependency and intent heads. The irreversible step therefore rests on a guarantee with an unspecified producer, two incompatible signing models and no owner for its only evaluator.

findings.where: 02-architecture.md:63-65 (§2: the ref-custody helper is the 'sole writer' of refs/autosk/** and project/model accounts 'cannot … invoke Git mutations') and docs/contracts/epic-staging.md:15 ('helper-owned prefix') vs 02-architecture.md:87, epic-staging.md:34 and ADR-088 (host swapTarget/applyDelta moves refs/autosk/epics/<key>/staging); resources/planning-publication/ref-custody-helper-wire.schema.json:54-62; src/host/staging-driver.mjs:104,183,206; src/host/planning-driver.mjs:131
findings.what: The custody chain for the private ref namespace contradicts itself. 02 §2 makes the separate-account helper the only writer of every create, CAS and delete under refs/autosk/**, and denies Git mutations to every other account. ADR-088, 02 §4 and epic-staging §1 assign the staging ref (refs/autosk/epics/<epic_ref_key>/staging) to the host's swapTarget, which runs git update-ref directly. The helper's closed wire protocol has six actions (init, create_keepalive, advance_planning, ensure_audit_ref, delete_live_ref, delete_expired_audit) and none for staging. The host planning driver, which says 'Implements: epic-planning-ref.md', also runs update-ref on the planning ref itself. An implementer cannot follow both rules: either the helper boundary is breached for staging, or staging has no writer. The foreign-movement and reflog guards on staging assume a custody model that the documents do not agree on.

findings.where: src/host/alignment-gates.mjs:254-274 (policyAlignment), 293-302 (gateAdmission) vs 01-core-flows.md §2 (table row for Brief: policy does not approve product framing; policy 'должна быть выдана через UserDecisionRecord'); package §5 'No user decision is accepted on any host'; ADR-091 open items
findings.what: The host's only alignment evaluator still has a second authority source with no signature. policyAlignment mints an 'authority: policy' record for any kind listed in a caller-supplied policy object, including brief. It checks no UserDecisionRecord that issued the policy and no project, Epic, scope or expiry binding. gateAdmission then admits that record, because it recomputes the identity with user_decision null against caller-supplied policy hashes. This contradicts 01 §2 and the 'one authority model' of 10e. ADR-091 lists it as open, but package §5 says that no host path accepts user authority today, which is overbroad.

findings.where: src/host/staging-acceptance.mjs:241, 285-289; 01-core-flows.md §7 (preamble, step 5); docs/contracts/integration-authorization.md §1; epic-staging.md §5
findings.what: The pinned auto-policy is described as a record signed in advance that lets the flow skip the human stop. assertAuthorized, however, requires the signed record's subject_hash, and the policy's pinned_identity, to equal stagingIdentity. That identity covers aggregate_record_hash, staging_commit_oid, outstanding_debt and delivery_profile_digest, which exist only after aggregate verification, at the stop itself. As specified, the user can sign only after the point the policy is meant to skip, so the auto path cannot exist without a human-timed signature. Either the design's 'in advance' claim or the binding is wrong.

findings.where: src/host/staging-driver.mjs:78 (readRef: oid.length === 40); src/host/planning-driver.mjs:61 (reflogEntries: line.length === 40)
findings.what: The host ref readers accept only SHA-1 OIDs, while the schemas, the helper wire protocol and 02 require handling both object formats. In a SHA-256 repository a present ref reads as null and every reflog as unknown, which turns foreign-movement detection into misclassification.
